questions.question: In the context of owner and weak entity sets in the ER (Entity-Relationship) data model, which one of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: The weak entity set MUST have total participation in the identifying relationship
options.B: The owner entity set MUST have total participation in the identifying relationship
options.C: Both weak and owner entity sets MUST have total participation in the identifying relationship
options.D: Neither weak entity set nor owner entity set MUST have total participation in the identifying relationship

questions.explanation:
A weak entity cannot exist without its owner, so every weak entity must take part in the identifying relationship [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] total participation of the weak entity set.

An owner may have no weak entities (e.g. an employee with no dependents), so the owner's participation is not necessarily total.

Answer: The weak entity set MUST have total participation in the identifying relationship

questions.question: Consider concurrent execution of two transactions [latex]T 1[/latex] and [latex]T 2[/latex] in a DBMS, both of which access a data object [latex]A[/latex]. For these two transactions to not conflict on [latex]A[/latex], which one of the following statements must be true?

options.B: [latex]T 1[/latex] reads [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]T 2[/latex] writes [latex]A[/latex]
options.C: [latex]T 1[/latex] writes [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]T 2[/latex] reads [latex]A[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Two operations by different transactions on the same data object [latex]A[/latex] "conflict" (in the standard DBMS concurrency-control sense) precisely when at least one of them is a write — i.e. any of read-write, write-read, or write-write pairs are conflicting, because the order in which they execute can change the outcome.

The only combination that never conflicts is when both transactions merely read [latex]A[/latex] — reads never interfere with each other regardless of execution order, since neither changes the value of [latex]A[/latex].

Answer: Both T1 and T2 only read A.

questions.question:
Consider the following two statements about database transaction schedules:

I. Strict two-phase locking protocol generates conflict serializable schedules that are also recoverable.
II. Timestamp-ordering concurrency control protocol with Thomas' Write Rule can generate view serializable schedules that are not conflict serializable.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?

options.B: II only
options.C: Both I and II

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until commit, so schedules are conflict serializable and no transaction reads uncommitted data [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] recoverable [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Thomas' write rule ignores obsolete writes, which allows some view serializable schedules that are not conflict serializable (blind writes) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Both I and II

questions.question:
A functional dependency [latex]F:X \rightarrow Y[/latex] is termed as a useful functional dependency if and only if it satisfies all the following three conditions:

[latex]X[/latex] is not the empty set. [latex]Y[/latex] is not the empty set. Intersection of [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] is the empty set.

For a relation [latex]R[/latex] with 4 attributes, the total number of possible useful functional dependencies is ______
questions.explanation:
X and Y must be non-empty and disjoint. Each of the 4 attributes goes to X, to Y, or to neither: [latex]3^4=81[/latex] ways.

Remove cases with X empty ([latex]2^4=16[/latex]) and Y empty ([latex]16[/latex]); add back both empty (1):
[latex]81-16-16+1=50[/latex]

Answer: 50

questions.question:
Consider the following database tables of a sports league.

player(pid,pname,age)
coach(cid,cname)
team(tid,tname,city,cid)
members(pid,tid)

An instance of the table and an SQL query are given.

The value returned by the given SQL query is _________. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
From the given table instances:
[latex]player[/latex]: (1,Jasprit,31), (2,Atharva,24), (3,Ishan,26), (4,Axar,30)
[latex]coach[/latex]: (101,Ricky), (102,Mark), (103,Trevor)
[latex]team[/latex]: (10,MI,Mumbai,102), (20,DC,Delhi,101), (30,PK,Mohali,103)
[latex]members[/latex]: (1,10), (2,30), (3,10), (4,20)

Evaluate the inner subquery first: [latex]C.cname=\text{'Mark'}[/latex] picks out coach [latex](102,\text{Mark})[/latex]. Then [latex]T.cid=C.cid=102[/latex] picks out team [latex](10,\text{MI},\text{Mumbai},102)[/latex]. Then [latex]M.tid=T.tid=10[/latex] picks out members with [latex]tid=10[/latex]: [latex]pid=1[/latex] and [latex]pid=3[/latex].

So the subquery returns [latex]\{1,3\}[/latex]. The outer query then computes [latex]\text{MIN(age)}[/latex] over players with [latex]pid\in\{1,3\}[/latex], i.e. Jasprit (age [latex]31[/latex]) and Ishan (age [latex]26[/latex]).

[latex]\text{MIN}(31,26)=26[/latex].

Answer: 26

questions.question:
Consider the following relational schema:

[latex] \text{Students} (\text{\underline{rollno: integer,} name: string, age: integer, cgpa: real}) [/latex]
[latex] \text{Courses} (\text{\underline{courseno: integer,} cname: string, credits: integer}) [/latex]
[latex] \text{Enrolled} (\text{ \underline{rollno: integer,} \underline{courseno: integer,} grade: string}) [/latex]

Which of the following options is/are correct SQL query/queries to retrieve the names of the students enrolled in course number (i.e. courseno) 1470?

options.A: SELECT S.name FROM Students S WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM Enrolled E WHERE E.courseno = 1470 AND E.rollno = S.rollno)
options.B: SELECT S.name FROM Students S WHERE SIZEOF (SELECT * FROM Enrolled E WHERE E.courseno = 1470 AND E.rollno = S.rollno) > 0
options.C: SELECT S.name FROM Students S WHERE 0 < (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Enrolled E WHERE E.courseno = 1470 AND E.rollno = S.rollno)
options.D: SELECT S.name FROM Students S NATURAL JOIN Enrolled E WHERE E.courseno = 1470

questions.explanation:
All of the standard relational-algebra-equivalent SQL formulations for "students who have an Enrolled row with courseno=1470" are valid: using [latex]\text{EXISTS}[/latex] with a correlated subquery, using [latex]\text{COUNT(*)} > 0[/latex] in place of EXISTS (logically identical test), and using a [latex]\text{NATURAL JOIN}[/latex] between Students and Enrolled (which automatically joins on the shared [latex]rollno[/latex] column) filtered by courseno — all three correctly retrieve the same set of names.

The option using [latex]\text{SIZEOF}[/latex] is not valid: standard SQL has no [latex]\text{SIZEOF}[/latex] operator/function for comparing subquery result sizes this way (that's not real SQL syntax).

Answer: The EXISTS query, the COUNT(*)>0 query, and the NATURAL JOIN query are all correct.

What does the above expression generate?

options.A: Employee numbers of only those employees whose age is the maximum
options.B: Employee numbers of only those employees whose age is more than the age of exactly one other employee
options.C: Employee numbers of all employees whose age is not the minimum
options.D: Employee numbers of all employees whose age is the minimum

questions.explanation:
The join pairs each employee with every employee who is younger (age [latex]\gt[/latex] age1). An employee appears in the result if at least one other employee is younger, i.e. if their age is not the minimum.

Answer: Employee numbers of all employees whose age is not the minimum

questions.question:
In a database system, unique time stamps are assigned to each transaction using Lamport's logical clock . Let TS([latex]T_{1}[/latex]) and TS([latex]T_{2}[/latex]) be the timestamps of transactions [latex]T_{1}[/latex] and [latex]T_{2}[/latex] respectively. Besides, [latex]T_{1}[/latex] holds a lock on the resource R, and [latex]T_{2}[/latex] has requested a conflicting lock on the same resource R. The following algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks in the database system assuming that a killed transaction is restarted with the same timestamp.

Assume any transactions that is not killed terminates eventually. Which of the following is TRUE about the database system that uses the above algorithm to prevent deadlocks?

options.A: The database system is both deadlock-free and starvation- free.
options.B: The database system is deadlock- free, but not starvation-free.
options.C: The database system is starvation-free but not deadlock- free.
options.D: The database system is neither deadlock- free nor starvation-free.

questions.explanation:
If the requester T2 is older (smaller timestamp), the younger holder T1 is killed; otherwise the younger requester waits. So a transaction only ever waits for an older one: no cycle of waits [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] deadlock-free.

A killed transaction restarts with its old timestamp, so it keeps getting older relative to new ones and eventually becomes the oldest, which is never killed [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] starvation-free.

Answer: both deadlock-free and starvation-free

questions.question:
Consider a relational database schema with two relations [latex]R(P, Q)[/latex] and [latex]S(X, Y)[/latex]. Let [latex]E=\{\langle u\rangle \mid \exists v \exists w\langle u, v\rangle \in R \wedge\langle v, w\rangle \in S\}[/latex] be a tuple relational calculus expression.
Which one of the following relational algebraic expressions is equivalent to [latex]E[/latex] ?

options.B: [latex]\Pi_{P}\left(S \bowtie_{S . X=R . Q} R\right)[/latex]
options.C: [latex]\Pi_{P}\left(R \bowtie_{R . P=S . Y} S\right)[/latex]

questions.explanation:
The calculus expression [latex]E=\{\langle u\rangle \mid \exists v\,\exists w\,\langle u,v\rangle\in R \wedge \langle v,w\rangle\in S\}[/latex] asks for all [latex]u[/latex] such that some tuple [latex]\langle u,v\rangle[/latex] is in [latex]R[/latex] and that same [latex]v[/latex] appears as the first component of some tuple [latex]\langle v,w\rangle[/latex] in [latex]S[/latex].

This is a natural join of [latex]R[/latex] and [latex]S[/latex] where [latex]R[/latex]'s second attribute ([latex]Q[/latex], which plays the role of [latex]v[/latex]) matches [latex]S[/latex]'s first attribute ([latex]X[/latex], which also plays the role of [latex]v[/latex]): join condition [latex]R.Q=S.X[/latex]. After joining, we only want the value of [latex]u[/latex], i.e. project onto [latex]P[/latex].

So [latex]E\equiv\Pi_P\big(S\bowtie_{S.X=R.Q}R\big)[/latex] (the join is symmetric, so writing [latex]S[/latex] first or [latex]R[/latex] first with the same condition gives the same relation).

Answer: [latex]\Pi_P\left(S\bowtie_{S.X=R.Q}R\right)[/latex]
